title: What I learned running an AI pipeline that ships a new puzzle game every hour (53 games, 3 AI raters each)
author: godivintech
selftext:
For the last couple of weeks I've been running an experiment: a scheduled Claude agent that, every hour, picks a theme from that hour's Google Trends (only the mood, never names, brands or people), designs a one-finger mobile puzzle, codes it as a single HTML file, generates levels, and publishes it to a small web gallery. 53 games so far. All the games are free to play here: [https://hyper.godivin.com/en/?ref=reddit-aigamedev](https://hyper.godivin.com/en/?ref=reddit-aigamedev)

How a run works:

1. Trend -> 3 ideas -> pick one. The agent has to read the previous raters' complaints first, so the pipeline is supposed to learn (it partly does).

2. Levels come from a generator plus a solver (BFS or a custom counter). Par = the shortest solution, and the stored solutions are replayed in Playwright to prove every level is solvable. This was the single biggest quality jump: before the solver rule, raters regularly hit unwinnable levels.

3. Three separate agents play it in a headless browser with different roles: player, publisher, designer. Each scores 1-10 on fixed criteria and writes a best/worst line. The builder then has to fix the top complaints before publishing.

4. Publish = Cloudflare Worker + catalog rebuild + SEO page in two languages.

What I learned:

\- The raters agree with each other a lot (usually within 0.3), which makes me suspect shared blind spots more than a reliable signal. Averages sit between 6.5 and 7.5; the best so far is 7.4.

\- Originality is the weakest score by far. Left alone, the agent keeps reinventing Flow Free, ball sort and pin pull with a new skin. Forcing a mechanic pool plus a 'do not repeat the last 5' rule helped a bit.

\- The same UX bugs come back in different games: the win panel covering the board, hints that are free forever, silent dead ends. Writing them into the prompt as hard rules worked better than relying on the raters.

\- Switching from hyper-casual action games to puzzles made everything better, because a solver gives you an objective check that 'fun' never does.

The best-rated ones if you want to judge for yourself: Net Loop (draw a net around fish), Lily Leap (frog peg solitaire), Mirror Waltz (swipe moves every dancer, partners mirror). The part I can't automate is real human opinion, so honest feedback is very welcome: are any of these actually good, or do they all feel the same?
